summary: Where two deserts meet: the higher Mojave, home of the shaggy Joshua tree, and the lower Colorado, with its cholla and ocotillo. Between them stand piles of granite boulders that draw climbers from around the world, under dark skies two hours from Los Angeles.
story: Elevation divides the park in two. Above about three thousand feet lies the Mojave Desert, cooler and wetter, where Joshua trees grow; below it, to the east, the hotter Colorado Desert, part of the Sonoran, with creosote bush, ocotillo and a garden of cholla cactus. The Little San Bernardino Mountains rise along the southwest edge.

The Joshua tree is a yucca, not a tree, and it depends entirely on a small moth to pollinate it. The name is said to come from Mormon emigrants, who saw a prophet's raised arms in its branches. Warming and drought now threaten the young trees, especially at lower elevations.

The park's boulders are granite that cooled deep underground, cracked into blocks, and was rounded by groundwater before erosion stripped away the soil around it. The result — Jumbo Rocks, Hidden Valley, the Wonderland of Rocks — is one of the most popular climbing areas in the country. Fan-palm oases grow where faults bring water to the surface.

The Pinto culture hunted here as long as ten thousand years ago; Serrano, Cahuilla and Chemehuevi people later lived near springs like the Oasis of Mara. Cattlemen, miners and homesteaders followed — Keys Ranch still stands. Minerva Hoyt, a Pasadena activist, persuaded President Franklin Roosevelt to proclaim a national monument in 1936, and the California Desert Protection Act made it a national park in 1994.

sights.name: Keys View
sights.note: A crest-top view over the Coachella Valley to the San Andreas Fault and the Salton Sea.

sights.name: Hidden Valley
sights.note: A boulder-ringed valley once used, the story goes, by cattle rustlers; an easy loop.

sights.name: Barker Dam
sights.note: A rancher-built dam that sometimes holds water, with petroglyphs nearby.

sights.name: Skull Rock
sights.note: A granite boulder weathered into the shape of a skull, beside the road at Jumbo Rocks.

sights.name: Cholla Cactus Garden
sights.note: A dense stand of teddybear cholla on a short loop trail, glowing at sunrise and sunset.

sights.name: Arch Rock
sights.note: A natural granite arch near White Tank Campground.

sights.name: Keys Ranch
sights.note: A homestead preserved as Bill Keys left it, seen on ranger-led tours.

sights.name: Lost Palms Oasis
sights.note: The park's largest grove of California fan palms, a long hike from Cottonwood Spring.

entrances: West Entrance, near the town of Joshua Tree on CA 62
North Entrance, at Twentynine Palms on CA 62
South Entrance, at Cottonwood Spring, from Interstate 10 exit 168
permits: Overnight backpacking — register at a backcountry board
lodging: No lodging in the park; towns along CA 62 and in the Coachella Valley
seasonalClosures: Summer days pass 100°F (38°C); winter nights freeze, and snow sometimes falls on the higher ground

chronology.text: A Spanish party led by Pedro Fages records the first European sighting of Joshua trees.
President Franklin Roosevelt proclaims Joshua Tree National Monument.
The California Desert Protection Act makes it a national park.

safety: Carry plenty of water and watch for signs of heat illness; there is little shade.
It is easy to get lost among the boulders. Note landmarks, and carry a map.
Cholla spines detach at a touch; give the plants room, and carry a comb to remove them.
regulations: Do not climb on or damage Joshua trees.
Drones may not be launched, landed or flown in the park.
